subject: science
title: Chemistry — The periodic table
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Chemistry — The periodic table, KS3 Science (National Curriculum).
meta_desc: KS3 Science practice covering Chemistry — The periodic table, from the National Curriculum programme of study.
final_note: You worked through Chemistry — The periodic table: 6 programme-of-study statements.

concepts.def: A substance made of only one type of atom. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by a chemical reaction. About 118 elements are known, and each has a symbol of one or two letters, the first a capital: O (oxygen), Na (sodium), Fe (iron).
concepts.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements

concepts.def: A property you can observe or measure without making a new substance: for example the state at room temperature, colour, shine, melting point, boiling point and whether the element conducts electricity.
concepts.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements

concepts.def: A property that shows how a substance reacts to make new substances. For example, magnesium burns in air to make magnesium oxide, and sodium reacts with water to make hydrogen and an alkaline solution.
concepts.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements

concepts.def: In a physical change, such as melting, boiling or dissolving, no new substance is made and the change can usually be reversed. In a chemical change (a reaction), such as burning, new substances are made.
concepts.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements

concepts.def: The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid. Elements' melting points vary hugely: mercury melts at −39 °C, sodium at 98 °C and iron at 1538 °C.
concepts.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements

concepts.def: The temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into a gas. An element is a liquid at room temperature if room temperature is above its melting point and below its boiling point: bromine melts at −7 °C and boils at 59 °C.
concepts.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements

concepts.def: In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements then known in order of atomic mass and put elements with similar properties in the same group. He left gaps for elements not yet discovered, predicted their properties, and swapped some pairs, such as tellurium and iodine, so that each element sat with similar elements.
concepts.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table

concepts.def: How heavy an atom of an element is compared with atoms of other elements (once called atomic weight). Hydrogen, the lightest, has an atomic mass of about 1, carbon about 12 and iodine about 127. Mendeleev used atomic masses to order the elements.
concepts.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table

concepts.def: The number that gives an element's place in today's periodic table, from hydrogen (1) upwards. Today's table is in order of atomic number. Mendeleev did not know about atomic numbers: they were worked out more than 40 years after his first table.
concepts.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table

concepts.def: A space Mendeleev left for an element he believed existed but had not yet been discovered. From the elements around each gap he predicted the missing element's properties; gallium (found in 1875), scandium (1879) and germanium (1886) later filled gaps and matched his predictions closely.
concepts.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table

concepts.def: A table of all the elements in order of atomic number, arranged in rows (periods) so that elements with similar properties line up in columns (groups).
concepts.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals

concepts.def: A vertical column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group react in similar ways. In UK school tables the main groups are numbered 1 to 7, then 0 for the noble gases.
concepts.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals

concepts.def: A horizontal row of the periodic table. Properties change across a period, from metals on the left to non-metals on the right: Period 3 runs from sodium, a reactive metal, to argon, an unreactive gas.
concepts.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals

concepts.def: The zig-zag line in the right-hand part of the periodic table. Metals are to its left and non-metals to its right; most elements are metals. Hydrogen is a non-metal, although tables usually show it away from the other non-metals.
concepts.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals

concepts.def: How readily and how vigorously an element reacts. Reactivity can be compared by watching reactions, for example how fast Group 1 metals fizz in water.
concepts.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table

concepts.def: Lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium and caesium are soft metals that react with water to make hydrogen and an alkaline solution. Reactivity increases going down the group: lithium fizzes gently, potassium bursts into lilac flames.
concepts.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table

concepts.def: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are coloured, reactive non-metals. Reactivity decreases going down the group, and their states change from gas (fluorine, chlorine) to liquid (bromine) to solid (iodine).
concepts.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table

concepts.def: Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon are colourless gases that hardly react at all. Argon is used inside some light bulbs because the hot filament does not react with it.
concepts.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table

concepts.def: Because elements in a group react in similar ways and follow a trend, you can predict how an element will react from its place in the table. A test then checks the prediction.
concepts.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table

concepts.def: An element to the left of the staircase line. Metals are typically shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable, and solid with high melting points. Exceptions: mercury is a liquid; sodium and potassium are soft and melt below 100 °C; only a few metals, such as iron, nickel and cobalt, are attracted to a magnet.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals

concepts.def: An element to the right of the staircase line, and hydrogen. Non-metals are typically dull and poor conductors of heat and electricity, and brittle when solid; many are gases. Exceptions: graphite, a form of carbon, conducts electricity, and graphite and iodine are shiny.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals

concepts.def: Able to be hammered or bent into a new shape without breaking. Most metals are malleable.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals

concepts.def: Breaks or shatters when hit or bent. Solid non-metals such as sulfur are brittle.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals

concepts.def: A conductor lets electricity (or heat) pass through it easily; an insulator does not. Metals are good conductors; most non-metals are insulators, but graphite conducts electricity.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals

concepts.def: A compound of an element with oxygen, often made by burning the element in air or oxygen: magnesium oxide, sulfur dioxide, carbon dioxide.
concepts.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity

concepts.def: A scale from 0 to 14 that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline. Universal indicator changes colour to show the pH.
concepts.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity

concepts.def: A substance that neutralises an acid. The oxides of metals such as sodium, calcium, magnesium and copper are bases.
concepts.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity

concepts.def: A base that dissolves in water, making an alkaline solution (pH above 7). Sodium oxide and calcium oxide dissolve to make alkaline solutions; copper oxide is a base that does not dissolve, so it is not an alkali.
concepts.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity

concepts.def: Oxides of metals such as sodium, calcium and copper are bases; those that dissolve make alkaline solutions. Oxides of non-metals that dissolve, such as sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide, make acidic solutions. A few non-metal oxides, such as water and carbon monoxide, are neutral.
concepts.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity

mcqs.q: Which of these shows a chemical property of an element?
options: Gallium melting in a person's hand
Iodine crystals dissolving in ethanol
Magnesium burning brightly in air
Iron and sulfur stirred together
mcqs.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
mcqs.explain: Yes. Burning makes a new substance, magnesium oxide, so it shows how magnesium reacts: a chemical property.
rationales: You may have thought melting changes gallium into something new. In fact melted gallium is still gallium and turns solid again when cooled; its low melting point (about 30 °C) is a physical property.
You may have thought dissolving makes a new substance. In fact the iodine is only spread through the ethanol; evaporating the ethanol gives the iodine back, so this is a physical change.
Yes. Burning makes a new substance, magnesium oxide, so it shows how magnesium reacts: a chemical property.
You may have thought mixing two elements makes a new substance. In fact stirring only mixes them, and a magnet can still pull out the iron; they react only when heated.

mcqs.q: Chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid at room temperature. All three are in Group 7. What does this show?
options: These three cannot really all be in one group
Their single atoms are a gas, a liquid and a solid
Only chlorine, as a gas, is a true non-metal
Elements in one group can be in different states
mcqs.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
mcqs.explain: Yes. Elements in a group react in similar ways, but their physical properties change going down the group: here from gas to liquid to solid.
rationales: You may have thought elements in a group must be identical. In fact they are similar in how they react, while their states and melting points change steadily going down the group.
You may have thought each atom has the state of its element. In fact gas, liquid and solid describe a sample made of huge numbers of particles, not a single atom.
You may have thought all non-metals are gases. In fact bromine (a liquid) and iodine (a solid) are non-metals too, just like chlorine.
Yes. Elements in a group react in similar ways, but their physical properties change going down the group: here from gas to liquid to solid.

mcqs.q: The chart shows the melting points of four metals. Which statement does the chart support?
options: All four of these metals are solids at 20 °C
Two of these metals melt below 100 °C
Each of these metals has a high melting point
A single atom of iron melts at 1538 °C
mcqs.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
mcqs.explain: Yes. Sodium melts at 98 °C and mercury at −39 °C, both below 100 °C. Metals' melting points vary hugely.
rationales: You may have thought every metal is a solid. In fact mercury melts at −39 °C, so at 20 °C it is already a liquid.
Yes. Sodium melts at 98 °C and mercury at −39 °C, both below 100 °C. Metals' melting points vary hugely.
You may have thought all metals melt only when very hot. In fact sodium melts at 98 °C and mercury at −39 °C, far lower than iron or copper.
You may have thought an atom has the properties of its element. In fact melting is something a piece of iron does; a single atom cannot melt.

mcqs.q: How did Mendeleev put the elements in order in his table?
options: By atomic mass, keeping similar elements together
By atomic number, as today's table does
By atomic mass alone, with no swaps made
By reactivity, from most to least reactive
mcqs.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
mcqs.explain: Yes. Mendeleev used atomic mass for the order, but put elements with similar properties in the same group, even if that meant swapping a pair.
rationales: Yes. Mendeleev used atomic mass for the order, but put elements with similar properties in the same group, even if that meant swapping a pair.
You may have thought Mendeleev used today's order. In fact atomic numbers were worked out more than 40 years after his 1869 table; he used atomic mass.
You may have thought he kept strictly to mass order. In fact he swapped some pairs, such as tellurium and iodine, so that each element sat with similar elements.
You may have mixed up the periodic table with the reactivity series. In fact Mendeleev ordered the elements by atomic mass and grouped similar ones together.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows part of the periodic table with today's atomic masses. Mendeleev put tellurium (Te) before iodine (I). Why?
options: He had misread the two atomic masses
He was ordering by atomic number
To put iodine with chlorine and bromine
So that the two columns would look neater
mcqs.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
mcqs.explain: Yes. Iodine's properties match chlorine and bromine, and tellurium's match sulfur and selenium. Mendeleev let properties decide the group, even though tellurium is heavier.
rationales: You may have thought any element out of mass order must be a mistake. In fact Mendeleev chose this order on purpose, so that each element sat in a group of similar elements.
You may have thought Mendeleev used atomic numbers. In fact these were not known in his time; he used atomic mass and swapped this pair because of their properties.
Yes. Iodine's properties match chlorine and bromine, and tellurium's match sulfur and selenium. Mendeleev let properties decide the group, even though tellurium is heavier.
You may have thought the layout was chosen to look tidy. In fact the swap followed the properties: iodine reacts like chlorine and bromine, not like sulfur and selenium.

mcqs.q: Mendeleev left a gap in the group with silicon and tin. What did he expect the missing element to be like?
options: Like the elements on either side in its row
Similar to silicon and tin in its group
Identical to silicon and tin in every way
Nothing could be said until it was found
mcqs.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
mcqs.explain: Yes. Elements in a group have similar properties, so he predicted an element like silicon and tin. Germanium, found in 1886, matched his predictions closely.
rationales: You may have thought elements next to each other in a row are alike. In fact similar elements are in the same column, so he used silicon and tin to make his prediction.
Yes. Elements in a group have similar properties, so he predicted an element like silicon and tin. Germanium, found in 1886, matched his predictions closely.
You may have thought elements in a group are identical. In fact they are only similar: he predicted values, such as its atomic mass, between those of silicon and tin.
You may have thought nothing can be known about an element until it is tested. In fact the pattern of the table let Mendeleev predict its properties years before germanium was found.

mcqs.q: Argon, the first noble gas to be collected, was found in 1894. Where were the noble gases in Mendeleev's first table, made in 1869?
options: In Group 0, just as in today's table
In the gaps he had left for them
At the end, as the least reactive
Nowhere: his table had no place for them
mcqs.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
mcqs.explain: Yes. Mendeleev did not know a whole group was missing, so his first table had no place for the noble gases. A new group, Group 0, was added later.
rationales: You may have thought the periodic table has not changed since Mendeleev. In fact Group 0 was added after the noble gases were discovered.
You may have thought Mendeleev left gaps for every element found later. In fact his gaps were for a few missing elements, such as germanium; he left no space for a whole new group.
You may have thought the periodic table is a list in order of reactivity. In fact Mendeleev's table was ordered by atomic mass, and it had no noble gases at all.
Yes. Mendeleev did not know a whole group was missing, so his first table had no place for the noble gases. A new group, Group 0, was added later.

mcqs.q: In the periodic table, what is a period?
options: A row of elements going across the table
A column of elements down the table
A family of elements that react alike
A list of elements in order of reactivity
mcqs.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
mcqs.explain: Yes. A period is a horizontal row. Properties change across a period, from metals on the left to non-metals on the right.
rationales: Yes. A period is a horizontal row. Properties change across a period, from metals on the left to non-metals on the right.
You may have mixed up the two words. A column is a group; a period is a row going across.
You may have thought the elements in a row are alike. In fact elements that react alike are in the same group (column); a period is a row.
You may have mixed up the periodic table with the reactivity series. In fact a period is simply a row of the table.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows an outline of the periodic table with one column shaded. Which statement about the shaded elements is correct?
options: They form one period of the table
They all react in a similar way
They are all gases at room temperature
They all have the same melting point
mcqs.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
mcqs.explain: Yes. The shaded column is a group (Group 7), and elements in the same group react in similar ways.
rationales: You may have mixed up groups and periods. A column is a group; a period is a row going across.
Yes. The shaded column is a group (Group 7), and elements in the same group react in similar ways.
You may have thought all non-metals are gases. In fact this is Group 7: chlorine is a gas, but bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid.
You may have thought elements in a group are identical. In fact their melting points rise going down Group 7, from gases at the top to solids lower down.

figure.alt: An outline of the periodic table made of small empty boxes in six rows, with the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 0 above the main columns and a wider block of unnumbered columns in the middle. A thick zig-zag staircase line runs down the right-hand part of the table. The whole column numbered 7, from the second row to the sixth, is shaded; all the shaded boxes are to the right of the staircase line.

mcqs.q: What does the staircase line on the periodic table separate?
options: Metal elements from non-metals
Reactive elements from unreactive ones
Solid elements from gaseous ones
Shiny elements from dull elements
mcqs.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
mcqs.explain: Yes. Metals are to the left of the staircase line and non-metals to its right. Most elements are metals.
rationales: Yes. Metals are to the left of the staircase line and non-metals to its right. Most elements are metals.
You may have thought only metals are reactive. In fact there are reactive and unreactive elements on both sides: fluorine and chlorine, to the right, are very reactive.
You may have thought the non-metals are all gases. In fact many non-metals to the right of the line, such as sulfur, carbon and iodine, are solids.
You may have thought being shiny decides whether an element is a metal. In fact iodine and graphite are shiny but are non-metals, to the right of the line.

mcqs.q: Potassium is below sodium in Group 1. Bromine is below chlorine in Group 7. Compared with the element above it, how reactive is each?
options: Potassium more; bromine more
Potassium less; bromine less
Potassium less; bromine more
Potassium more; bromine less
mcqs.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
mcqs.explain: Yes. Going down Group 1 the metals get more reactive, so potassium beats sodium. Going down Group 7 the halogens get less reactive, so bromine is less reactive than chlorine.
rationales: You may have thought every group gets more reactive going down, like Group 1. In fact Group 7 goes the other way: bromine is less reactive than chlorine.
You may have thought the top element of every group is the most reactive. That is true for Group 7 but not Group 1: potassium is more reactive than sodium.
You may have swapped the two trends. Going down Group 1, reactivity increases; going down Group 7, it decreases.
Yes. Going down Group 1 the metals get more reactive, so potassium beats sodium. Going down Group 7 the halogens get less reactive, so bromine is less reactive than chlorine.

mcqs.q: Rubidium is just below potassium in Group 1. How will rubidium react with water, compared with potassium?
options: Less vigorously, as the top one reacts most
Just as vigorously, as it is in one group
More vigorously, as it is lower in the group
Unknown, as only a test can show this
mcqs.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
mcqs.explain: Yes. Reactivity increases going down Group 1, so rubidium reacts even more violently than potassium, making hydrogen and an alkaline solution.
rationales: You may have thought the top of every group is the most reactive. In Group 1 it is the other way: reactivity increases going down.
You may have thought elements in a group react identically. In fact they react in similar ways, but reactivity changes steadily going down the group.
Yes. Reactivity increases going down Group 1, so rubidium reacts even more violently than potassium, making hydrogen and an alkaline solution.
You may have thought nothing can be said before a test. In fact the Group 1 trend lets you predict that rubidium reacts more vigorously; a test would confirm it.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows how hot iron wool reacts with three Group 7 elements. Fluorine is above chlorine. Predict how hot iron wool reacts with fluorine.
options: Less strongly than it does with iodine
Even more strongly than with chlorine
Exactly as strongly as with chlorine
Nothing can be said without a test
mcqs.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
mcqs.explain: Yes. The results show reactivity falling going down Group 7, so fluorine, above chlorine, reacts most strongly of all: iron wool burns in it.
rationales: You may have thought every group gets more reactive going down, like Group 1. The results show the opposite for Group 7, so fluorine reacts most strongly.
Yes. The results show reactivity falling going down Group 7, so fluorine, above chlorine, reacts most strongly of all: iron wool burns in it.
You may have thought elements in a group react identically. The results show a steady change down the group, so fluorine should react even more strongly than chlorine.
You may have thought you cannot say anything before testing. In fact the trend in the results lets you predict a stronger reaction; a test would check it.

figure.alt: A column headed Group 7 with four boxes from top to bottom: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine. Beside each box, under the heading hot iron wool, is what happens: fluorine, ? (not tested); chlorine, bright glow spreads quickly; bromine, glows, less brightly; iodine, little or no glow.

mcqs.q: Sodium burns in chlorine. Xenon is in Group 0, below krypton. Predict what happens when sodium is heated in xenon.
options: It burns, as xenon is a gas like chlorine
It reacts, as xenon is low in its group
Unknown until someone has tested it
No reaction, as xenon is a noble gas
mcqs.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
mcqs.explain: Yes. The Group 0 elements, the noble gases, hardly react at all, so sodium will not burn in xenon as it does in chlorine.
rationales: You may have thought elements in the same state behave alike. In fact chlorine is a reactive halogen in Group 7, while xenon is an unreactive noble gas in Group 0.
You may have thought reactivity increases going down every group. That is the Group 1 trend; the Group 0 elements hardly react at all, wherever they are in the group.
You may have thought nothing can be said before a test. In fact xenon's place in Group 0 lets you predict that it will not react.
Yes. The Group 0 elements, the noble gases, hardly react at all, so sodium will not burn in xenon as it does in chlorine.

mcqs.q: Which property do all metals have?
options: They are attracted to a magnet
They are solid at room temperature
They can conduct electricity
They have high melting points
mcqs.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
mcqs.explain: Yes. Every metal conducts electricity. Most metals are solid and hard, but not all, and only a few, such as iron, are attracted to a magnet.
rationales: You may have thought all metals are magnetic. In fact only a few, such as iron, nickel and cobalt, are; copper, aluminium and gold are not.
You may have thought every metal is a solid. In fact mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Yes. Every metal conducts electricity. Most metals are solid and hard, but not all, and only a few, such as iron, are attracted to a magnet.
You may have thought all metals melt only when very hot. In fact sodium melts at 98 °C and potassium at 64 °C.

mcqs.q: The table shows some properties of four elements. Which conclusion does the table support?
options: A non-metal can still conduct electricity
Iodine is a metal, as it is shiny
Carbon must be a metal, as it conducts
Mercury is not a metal, as it is liquid
mcqs.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
mcqs.explain: Yes. Carbon is a non-metal, yet graphite conducts electricity. Typical properties of non-metals have exceptions.
rationales: Yes. Carbon is a non-metal, yet graphite conducts electricity. Typical properties of non-metals have exceptions.
You may have thought anything shiny is a metal. In fact iodine is a non-metal in Group 7: it is shiny but does not conduct electricity.
You may have thought non-metals can never conduct. In fact carbon is a non-metal, to the right of the staircase line, and graphite still conducts.
You may have thought every metal must be solid. In fact mercury is a metal: it is shiny and conducts electricity, but it is liquid at 20 °C.

mcqs.q: Sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife and melts at 98 °C. Is sodium a metal?
options: Yes: each sodium atom is soft and shiny
No: metals are hard and difficult to melt
Yes: it is one of the alkali metals
No: a magnet does not attract it
mcqs.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
mcqs.explain: Yes. Sodium is in Group 1, the alkali metals, and it is shiny when cut and conducts electricity. Not every metal is hard with a high melting point.
rationales: You may have thought single atoms have the properties of the element. Sodium is a metal, but softness and shine belong to a piece of sodium, not to one atom.
You may have thought all metals are hard and melt only when very hot. In fact the Group 1 metals, such as sodium, are soft and melt at low temperatures.
Yes. Sodium is in Group 1, the alkali metals, and it is shiny when cut and conducts electricity. Not every metal is hard with a high melting point.
You may have thought all metals are magnetic. In fact only a few metals, such as iron, are attracted to a magnet; sodium is a metal that is not.

mcqs.q: Sodium oxide and calcium oxide are metal oxides that dissolve in water. What do they form?
options: An alkaline solution
An acidic solution
Just a neutral solution
Hydrogen and an alkali
mcqs.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
mcqs.explain: Yes. These metal oxides are bases, and because they dissolve they make alkaline solutions, with a pH above 7.
rationales: Yes. These metal oxides are bases, and because they dissolve they make alkaline solutions, with a pH above 7.
You may have reversed the rule. It is non-metal oxides, such as sulfur dioxide, that make acidic solutions; metal oxides make alkaline ones.
You may have thought metal oxides are neutral. In fact these metal oxides are bases, and as they dissolve they make the water alkaline.
You may have thought the oxide reacts like the metal, giving off hydrogen. In fact no hydrogen forms: the oxide simply makes an alkaline solution.

mcqs.q: Element X burns in oxygen. Its oxide dissolves in water, making a solution of pH 3. What is X most likely to be?
options: A metal, since metal oxides are acidic
A metal, as non-metals do not burn
Either, as all oxides are acidic
A non-metal, as its oxide is acidic
mcqs.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
mcqs.explain: Yes. pH 3 is acidic, and non-metal oxides, such as sulfur dioxide, make acidic solutions. X is most likely a non-metal such as sulfur.
rationales: You may have reversed the rule. Metal oxides that dissolve make alkaline solutions; acidic solutions come from non-metal oxides.
You may have thought non-metals are too unreactive to burn. In fact non-metals such as sulfur and carbon burn in oxygen, and their oxides make acidic solutions.
You may have thought every oxide is acidic. In fact metal oxides that dissolve make alkaline solutions, so an acidic solution points to a non-metal.
Yes. pH 3 is acidic, and non-metal oxides, such as sulfur dioxide, make acidic solutions. X is most likely a non-metal such as sulfur.

mcqs.q: Copper oxide powder is stirred with water and filtered. The filtered water has pH 7. What is copper oxide?
options: A neutral oxide, as the water is pH 7
A base, as it can neutralise acids
An acidic oxide, like any oxide
An alkali, as it is a metal oxide
mcqs.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
mcqs.explain: Yes. Copper oxide neutralises acids, for example making copper sulfate with sulfuric acid, so it is a base. It does not dissolve, so the water stays at pH 7.
rationales: You may have thought pH 7 shows that copper oxide is neutral. In fact it only shows that copper oxide did not dissolve; it still neutralises acids, so it is a base.
Yes. Copper oxide neutralises acids, for example making copper sulfate with sulfuric acid, so it is a base. It does not dissolve, so the water stays at pH 7.
You may have thought every oxide is acidic. In fact copper oxide is the oxide of a metal, and it neutralises acids, so it is a base.
You may have thought base and alkali mean the same. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water; copper oxide does not dissolve, so it is a base but not an alkali.

mcqs.q: Element W is dull and grey. It conducts electricity, a magnet does not attract it, and it can be hammered flat. What is W?
options: A metal, as only metals conduct electricity
A non-metal, as it is dull, not shiny
A metal, as it is malleable and conducts
A non-metal, as magnets do not attract it
mcqs.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
mcqs.explain: Yes. Being malleable (it can be hammered flat without breaking) and conducting electricity are typical of metals. A metal's surface often looks dull after it has reacted with the air.
rationales: You may have thought only metals conduct electricity. W is a metal, but not for that reason: graphite, a non-metal, conducts too. It is being malleable as well that marks W as a metal.
You may have thought one property, being dull, decides it. In fact a metal's surface often goes dull in air; W conducts and can be hammered flat, so it is a metal.
Yes. Being malleable (it can be hammered flat without breaking) and conducting electricity are typical of metals. A metal's surface often looks dull after it has reacted with the air.
You may have thought every metal is attracted to a magnet. In fact only a few metals, such as iron, nickel and cobalt, are; W is a metal that is not.

specSource: National Curriculum in England, key stage 3 science — Chemistry; Chemistry — The periodic table (DfE 2013 programme of study, verbatim)

specStatements.text: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
the properties of metals and non-metals
the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity

scopeNotes.decision: Elements differ in physical properties (state at room temperature, appearance, melting point, conductivity) and chemical properties (how they react to make new substances); items ask students to tell a physical property from a chemical one and to read given data.
scopeNotes.basis: The key stage 3 programme of study gives no depth for this heading. Explaining properties by structure and bonding (metallic, covalent and giant structures) is GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept, misconception or rationale explains a property using bonding, structure or electrons. Every melting or boiling point used is an accepted value rounded to the nearest whole degree: iron 1538 °C, copper 1085 °C, sodium 98 °C, potassium 64 °C, gallium about 30 °C, mercury −39 °C, bromine −7 °C (boils at 59 °C).

scopeNotes.decision: Mendeleev's principles are tested: he ordered the elements by atomic mass, put elements with similar properties in the same group, swapped some pairs (tellurium and iodine) to keep groups consistent, left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties; his first table had no noble gases. Atomic number is named only as the order of today's table.
scopeNotes.basis: Atomic number as the number of protons, and isotopes as the reason why atomic-mass order sometimes fails, belong to the GCSE topic on the development of the periodic table (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept, misconception or rationale mentions protons, electrons, isotopes or what atomic number counts; atomic number appears only as the order used in today's table. Atomic masses in the one figure that shows them are labelled as today's values.

scopeNotes.decision: Groups are columns and periods are rows; elements in a group react in similar ways; metals lie to the left of the staircase line and non-metals to its right, with most elements being metals.
scopeNotes.basis: Explaining groups by electron arrangement is GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015). UK school tables number the main groups 1 to 7 and 0, as the site's lesson does.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Groups are named 1 to 7 and 0 throughout. No item explains group membership or the staircase line by electrons or outer shells, and no item asks about the transition metals as a group.

scopeNotes.decision: Predictions use group patterns: reactivity increases going down Group 1, decreases going down Group 7, and Group 0 elements are unreactive; elements in a group react in similar ways, so an untested element's behaviour can be predicted from its neighbours and from given observations.
scopeNotes.basis: Explaining these trends by electron shells or the distance of outer electrons from the nucleus is GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015, 'Group 1', 'Group 7').
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Trends are stated and used, never explained: no item, concept, misconception or rationale gives an electron-based reason for a trend or for the unreactivity of the noble gases.

scopeNotes.decision: Typical properties of metals (shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable, mostly solid with high melting points) and of non-metals (dull, poor conductors, brittle when solid, many are gases) are tested together with real exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal, sodium and potassium are soft with low melting points, graphite conducts, iodine and graphite are shiny, and only a few metals are magnetic.
scopeNotes.basis: Metallic bonding and delocalised electrons as the explanation of metal properties are GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015); the KS3 programme of study does not name metalloids.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept, misconception or rationale mentions bonding, electrons or metalloids. Every exception used is a real element: mercury, sodium, potassium, graphite (carbon) and iodine. One item uses a hypothetical element W whose stated properties (dull grey surface, conducts, not magnetic, malleable) are those of a real metal such as lead.

scopeNotes.decision: Metal oxides are bases, and those that dissolve in water (sodium oxide, calcium oxide) make alkaline solutions; copper oxide does not dissolve but still neutralises acids; non-metal oxides that dissolve (sulfur dioxide, carbon dioxide) make acidic solutions. Neutral and amphoteric oxides are not tested.
scopeNotes.basis: The programme of study says only 'with respect to acidity'. The RSC practical 'Testing the pH of oxides' states the KS3 point as 'the soluble oxides of metals are alkaline and the oxides of non-metals are acidic'; amphoteric oxides and acid–base ionic equations are GCSE or A-level content.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every oxide named in an item or its rationales is sodium oxide, calcium oxide, magnesium oxide, copper oxide, sulfur dioxide or an unnamed oxide of a hypothetical element X. No item uses ions, ionic equations, or a neutral or amphoteric oxide as the tested idea.
